# vervets <a href='https://fuzzyatelin.github.io/vervets/'><img src='man/figures/vervets_badge_bg.png' align="right" height="138.5" /></a>

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->

The goal of *vervets* is to provide users with an easy and simple way to learn about and use the extensive datasets and samples of wild savanna monkeys (*Chlorocebus* spp., also commonly called "vervets") generated by the **International Vervet Research Consortium (IVRC)**.

In this package, you'll find datasets for both teaching and exploration, as well as datasets intended to help you design research projects with publicly available resources. These datasets may also be linked to several others that are publicly available in external online repositories (like [EnsEMBL](https://useast.ensembl.org/Chlorocebus_sabaeus/Info/Index) and [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/search/all/?term=Chlorocebus)). The package will make clear when it needs to link out to external resources (which may require an internet connection during use).

This package is currently in the early stages of development, so more to come!

![](img/humbert_soetdoring.png)

## Installation

You can install the development version of *vervets* from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("fuzzyatelin/vervets")
```

## About the Data

<img src="img/vervet_map.png" alt="IVRC collection sites, from Turner et al. (2018)" align="right" style="margin-left: 10px; width: 350px;"> 

The IVRC data represent body measurements, photographs, and a comprehensive set of biological samples and their derived data (i.e., genome sequence data, gene expression data, microbiome data, hormone data, and more) from over 2,300 wild savanna monkeys (*Chlorocebus* spp.) representing numerous taxa across Africa and the Caribbean (see inset map), collected by numerous associated research groups over the course of decades of research. These data have been compiled and made available for use within this package by IVRC member [Dr. Christopher A. Schmitt](https://www.evopropinquitous.net) and founder [Dr. Trudy Turner](https://uwm.edu/anthropology/people/turner-trudy-r/). You can learn more about how the data were collected in one of the IVRC's summary papers by [Jasinska *et al.* (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1093/ilar/ilt049), in our book, [*Savanna Monkeys*](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781139019941), and the associated publication for this package by [Schmitt *et al.* (2027)]().

These numerous datasets are linked by two important indexing columns:

* The first is an `animal_id`, which identifies individual monkeys and allows you to link numerous potential datasets that are derived from measurements or samples collected on that individual monkey. 
* The second is a `collection`, which identifies a particular research effort or field season that resulted in the collection of associated sets of measurements, biological samples, and downstream data.

The distinction between these two identifiers is important given that *data from different collections may be subject to different constraints or methods*, even if collected on the same monkey at the same research site.

<div style="clear: both;"></div>

Within the *vervets* package itself, there are several datasets, from which we've derived several helpful subsets to walk you through the utility of the IVRC data:
```{r, eval=F}
library(vervets)
data(package = 'vervets')
```

One is called `vervets`, and is a simplified version of the larger raw dataset showing the availability of samples and data for each individual across all collections; see `?vervets` for more info:
```{r, eval=F}
head(vervets)
```

The other is called `vervets_raw`, and contains all the variables and names as originally downloaded; see `?vervets_raw` for more info:
```{r, eval=F}
head(vervets_raw)
```

Both datasets contain, in all, information on sample and data availability for 2,315 savanna monkeys that have been sampled by the IVRC from across Africa and the Caribbean.

Our hope is that you can use the *vervets* package to design experiments with the IVRC data (and not just *in silico* with the in-package datasets, although we hope you'll do that too). The `vervets` dataset is here to help you design and generate potential research proposals that take advantage of our extensive sample archives, as well. Please check out `vignette("vervets")` for basic guidance on the overall dataset and how to use it for sample queries and project design.

For example, by visualizing the sample size of individuals from a particular `collection` that have shared sample types available you could design a multi-omics project with whole genome, RNA-seq, and serum metabolomic data, the results of which you could validate in a fibroblast-based cell line system. Based on our data, you'd have a strong sample size for such a project in the vervet collection from South Africa in 2010 (n = 199); but not so strong for the vervets collection from The Gambia in 2011 (n = 9):

![](img/vervsamples_ucla.png)

The metadata available within *vervets* will guide you towards whom to contact and where the samples are available so that you can take your project idea from planning to implementation!


### Morphological Datasets

We've included potentially helpful subsets of cleaned morphometic data that, in addition to addressing novel research questions, may be used to teach and/or replicate key analyses from papers published by IVRC members.

<img src="img/vervet_measures.png" alt="IVRC morphometic measures, from Turner et al. (1997)" align="left" style="margin-right: 15px; margin-top: 15px; width: 250px;"> 

These include `vervmorph`, a comprehensive morphological dataset, sourced from our published dataset on [Dryad](https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.vt4b8gtss), which will be updated with comparable morphological data from future collections:
```{r, eval=F}
head(vervmorph)
```

And two subsidiary datasets derived from published IVRC analyses that can be used for teaching and replication:

<div style="clear: both;"></div>

* `turner97`, representing a subset of 367 vervet monkeys from four sites in Kenya, which can be used to replicate the [Turner *et al.* (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1096-8644(199705)103:1%3C19::AID-AJPA3%3E3.0.CO;2-8) paper on vervet monkey body size and growth.

<img src="img/turner_massmorph.png" alt="Growth modeled for body pass from IVRC morphometic measures, from Turner et al. (2018)" align="right" style="margin-left: 10px; margin-top: 10px; width: 400px;"> 

* `turner18`, representing a subset of 1,253 savanna monkeys from four taxa (*C. aethiops* in Ethiopia, *C. pygerythrus hilgerti* in Kenya, *C. pygerythrus pygerythrus* in South Africa, and *C. sabaeus* in St. Kitts & Nevis), which can be used to replicate results from the [Turner *et al.* (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.23459) paper on variation in savanna monkey body size and growth.

<div style="clear: both;"></div>

You can use `vignette("vervet_morphometrics")` for guidance on how to access and use these morphological datasets.

For the collection of savanna monkey morphological data, we follow the protocol recommendations of the [Bones and Behavior Working Group](https://wp.nyu.edu/csho/research/bones-and-behavior-working-group/) for standardized anthropometric body measurements on living non-human primates. For more details, you can also see the methods outlined by Turner *et al.* (1997), and further described by Turner *et al.* (2018). 

### Genetic/Genomic Datasets

<img src="img/gagnon_genomics.png" alt="Vervet genetic variation in UCP1, from Gagnon et al. (2022)" align="right" style="margin-left: 20px; margin-bottom: 20px; margin-top: 10px; width: 400px;">

One of the key foci of the IVRC was to develop savanna monkeys as a genetic/genomic resource, for both biomedical and evolutionary biology research. We chose savanna monkeys, in part, due to their relatively unique population history, which makes them particularly compelling as a genetic model system. Their wide ecogeographic range across Africa presents a variety of evolutionary questions regarding how they manage to thrive in riparian forests throughout savannah landscapes in highly variable climates south of the Sahara, ranging from The Gambia across the Sahel to Kenya, and from Ethiopia to South Africa along the Indian Ocean coast (the result of rapid expansion and diversification from their West African origins during the Plio-Pleistocene). The reduced genetic diversity presented by a key bottleneck that occurred when green monkeys (*Chlorocebus sabaeus*) were opportunistically brought to the Caribbean from West Africa ~400 years ago additionally makes them a great model system in which to establish connections between phenotypic trait variation and the genetic variation that might underlie it.

<div style="clear: both;"></div>

#### Captive Genetic/Genomic Data

A second major bottleneck occurred when 67 of monkeys from St. Kitts were brought to the United States to create a captive research colony at the University of California - Los Angeles in the mid-1970's. The [Vervet Research Colony](https://school.wakehealth.edu/departments/pathology/comparative-medicine/vervet-research-colony) (now housed at the Wake Forest School of Medicine) is a captive breeding colony of ~250 green monkeys with an extensive pedigree dating back to the initial founding of the colony. With over 1,000 monkeys pedigreed, 721 of which are whole genome sequenced (with many more in process), the colony is a fantastic system for investigating genetic links to behavior and biology, particularly in biomedical contexts. The VRC data, however, are generally not publicly available and so are not currently accessible in the *vervets* package.

Contact [Dr. Matt Jorgensen](https://school.wakehealth.edu/faculty/j/matthew-j-jorgensen) for questions regarding access to VRC datasets.

#### Wild Genetic/Genomic Data

![](img/svardal_genomics.png)

The IVRC has generated both a [reference sequence (ChlSab 1.1)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26377836/) and [whole genome population resequencing data](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29083404/) for 163 wild savanna monkeys. Including the raw sequencing reads from these efforts in the *vervets* package would make it prohibitively large, but the package does include instructions for how to access those raw data for download (i.e., links to SRAs in free online repositories) and for accessing the VCF (Variant Call Format) for the whole genome data generated by [Svardal et al. (2017)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29083404/), which is available on the European Variant Archive ([PRJEB22988](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/eva/?eva-study=PRJEB22988)). A population panel, `svardal17pop`, is included in this package, which can be paired with this whole genome VCF file to facilitate phenotype matching to the genomic data.

We also include in the *vervets* package a published VCF dataset representing population resequencing data in the *UCP1* gene region for 73 savanna monkeys representing the southern expansion of the genus into colder southern Africa, called `Gagnon22vcf`, along with an associated vervet population panel file, called `Gagnon22pop`, to link sex and population assignments to the VCF data. `vignette("vervet_genomics")` will walk you through the analyses from [Gagnon *et al.*, 2022](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspb.2022.1254), and for working with the vervet genomic data, in general. This relatively simple *UCP1* data can be used as a teaching dataset for population genetics, and to prepare you for tackling the larger genomics dataset. 

Similarly derived subsets of the vervet genomic data - the collection of which may be facilitated by `vignette("vervet_genomics")` - may also be combined with our other datasets to set up novel analyses of how genetic variation may vary across populations in relation to other climatic or phenotypic data (as done for heat shock protein *HSPA1L* by [Dippel *et al.* 2026](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4425/17/12/1492)).


### Biological Sample Repositories

When IVRC members trap vervets, we collect a wide variety of biological samples to make the most of our efforts. Although many samples are immediately slated for processing to answer specific questions, many of these processes either do not use up a whole sample, or may use some derivative of a sample leaving a lot of biological material left over that can be used in other analyses. A major goal of the 'vervets' package is to help make other researchers aware of the samples available, and encourage them to design potential experiments with available archived samples so that they might be put to use!

![](img/ivrc_samples.png)

At the moment, we have four major sample archives, each with numerous sample types:

* **The International Vervet Research Consortium Sample Archive** is held by the [Biological Samples Processing Core](https://www.semel.ucla.edu/research/core/biological-samples-processing-core-–-bspc) at UCLA's Semel Institute for Neuroscience and Human Behavior in Los Angeles, California in the United States. This public archive was generated by NIH funding (R01RR0163009; 2T32NS048004-06A1) and is the result of years of intensive sampling of over 2,500 wild savanna monkeys (*Chlorocebus* spp.) across Africa and the Caribbean. The majority of the archive was generated by researchers at the UCLA Center for Neurobehavioral Genetics, the University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee, and the University of the Free State (South Africa), in association with the IVRC. It is comprised of fibroblast cell lines, blood samples (PAXgene DNA, PAXgene RNA, plasma clots, serum clots, spun down plasma, spun down serum), tissue samples (3mm ear punches), and microbiome swabs (vaginal, rectal, tongue, buccal, nasal), and fecal samples stored in both RNAlater and ethanol. Currently, this sample archive is under the curation of [Dr. Anna Jasinska](https://www.profiles.dom.pitt.edu/faculty_info.aspx/Jasinska7405) (University of Pittsburgh). Associated hair samples and dried blood spots from these collections are held at Boston University in the Trudy Turner Vervet Monkey Sample Archive.

* **The Trudy Turner Vervet Monkey Sample Archive** is held at the Sensory Morphology and Anthropological Genomics Lab (SMAGL) at Boston University in Boston, Massachusetts in the United States, and curated by [Dr. Christopher A. Schmitt](https://www.evopropinquitous.net). This public sample archive was generated by Trudy R. Turner (Distinguished Professor Emeritis at University of Wisconsin, Milwaukee) in the course of over 60 years of working with wild savanna monkeys (*Chlorocebus* spp.), including a large portion generated while leading field collections with the IVRC. The archive is comprised of thousands of wild vervet samples from across Africa and the Caribbean, predominantly clipped fur samples and dried blood spots. These samples were generated by funding from the NIH (R01RR01163009), NSF (SOC-74-24166, BNS-770-3322, BCS-0938969), the University of Wisconsin – Milwaukee, the University of the Free State (South Africa), the University of Limpopo (South Africa), and the Coriell Institute.

* **The Vervet Monkey Plasma Clot Archive** is held by the [University of Pretoria Veterinary Genetics Lab](https://www.up.ac.za/the-onderstepoort-veterinary-genetics-laboratory) in Onderstepoort, South Africa. This archive was begun in association with the production of STR/microsatellite markers from wild vervet monkeys (*Chlorocebus pygerythrus pygerythrus*) collected in Soetdoring Nature Reserve, a private farm in Gariep Dam, and Sandveld Nature Reserve, South Africa. These markers were generated from plasma clots from wild collections associated with the BU/NWU Vervet Monkey Sample Archive, and generated by funding from Boston University. In agreement with UPVGL standards the source clots are now part of their public sample archive and under their curation.

* **The BU/NWU Vervet Monkey Sample Archive** is currently held at the Microbiology Department of North-West University in Potchefstroom, South Africa (soon to be accessioned into the [South African National Biodiversity Institute](https://www.sanbi.org)). This soon-to-be public sample archive is generated by and under the curation of [Dr. Christopher A. Schmitt](https://www.evopropinquitous.net) at Boston University and [Prudent Mokgokong](https://natural-sciences.nwu.ac.za/unit-environmental-sciences-and-management/prudent-mokgokong) at North-West University.  The archive includes all physical data collected during their research on wild vervet monkeys (*Chlorocebus pygerythrus pygerythrus*) in South Africa. The archive is comprised of blood samples (PAXgene DNA, PAXgene RNA, plasma clots, serum clots, spun down plasma, spun down serum), tissue samples (3mm ear punches), hair samples, dried blood spots, microbiome swabs (vaginal, rectal, tongue, buccal, nasal), and fecal samples stored in both RNAlater and ethanol. Although these samples will be embargoed while still being analyzed by BU/NWU, they will become a public archive under SANBI curation upon associated publication. These samples were generated by funding from Boston University, The Leakey Foundation, and the National Geographic Society.

### Other Datasets

Additional datasets have been or are in the process of being generated from our standing biological sample repositories that are associated with those already present in the 'vervets' package! Typically, we wait until collaborators have the chance to publish based on any newly-generated data prior to adding them to the package. Once those collaborators publish, however, we plan to integrate them into the package so they will be similarly available and/or at least linked to the already-existing dataset. 

Coming additions for future builds of this package may include or direct users to links to:

* Hormone data derived from hair (testosterone, cortisol, progesterone)
* Mitogenome sequence data
* Gut microbiome data
* Oral microbiome data
* Vaginal microbiome data
* Novel morphometric data from wild South African vervets

Please do not ask the package maintainers regarding when those data will be added; package updates will make it clear when they have become available! 

## License

Please note that the data contained in the *vervets* package are released under the terms of a Creative Commons Zero (CC0) waiver. In doing so, we concur with Dryad's logic regarding why this was chosen, which you can read more about [here](https://blog.datadryad.org/2011/10/05/why-does-dryad-use-cc0/). In keeping with the norms of our academic discipline, we humbly ask that you cite any associated papers when using data from *vervets* in your own publications.

## Citation

To cite the *vervets* package, please use:

```{r,eval=F}
citation("vervets")
```

## Additional Data Use Information

Anyone interested in publishing based on these data should contact [Dr. Christopher Schmitt](https://www.evopropinquitous.net) about analysis and potential collaboration on any final products. This is recommended beyond appropriate citation of associated literatures because we may know nuances about the dataset you're using that might be important for your analyses!
